title: Any Guidance on using Claude Code with Unity?
author: ChaosMilkTea
selftext:
I've been experimenting with using Claude Code with the Unity engine, and I have slowly started to develop a decent system where I could talk out the code/implementation, reason out what scripts I wanted and where that code would live, and then script by script Claude would explain how it would write them and if I agreed it would write them into the game. If there was anything I didn't understand, I could ask Claude to explain it. At some point I hooked up the MPC so it could run tests in engine which helped a ton with bug fixing.  It works, but I've just kind of been winging it. I want to make sure I'm getting the most out of an AI assisted workflow.

Anyone got advice? Are there guides? Youtube videos?

comments.author: DaedalusRaistlin
comments.body:
I just use the Claude desktop app in code mode. It connects to the MCP fine. 

One neat ability is that you can pause the game when playing in the editor, with a problem in view, and get Claude to look at the scene to diagnose what problem you're encountering. It was very helpful in the building destruction system I'm making, I could find an anomoly like some floors still rendering, or physics happening out of order, a d pause the editor and complain to Claude about it. It could figure out from the game state what and why was happening and write a fix for it. 

I've also had it write a few useful tools for Unity that are now shared across all my games:

* An asset explorer showing models and scenes and letting me mark them on a scale of how much I want them in the project and I can add notes on what I like about the or if they're unsuitable. Claude can pull from these after my review to populate scenes. It can make a sample gallery if the pack didn't come with one. 

* A fix the purple textures button

* An asset report showing how much space everything we're deploying takes 

* A button to add a simple camera and player controller to a scene (usually an asset demo scene) 

Agents can test your game in the editor over MCP, as well as in web builds using CDP (Chrome something Protocol.) 

It's not all that much different for me than making games for Three.js. I still use both.

comments.author: samu-physicist
comments.body:
I'm on Godot rather than Unity, but the workflow layer transfers. About a month into a solo project with Claude Code, these moved the needle most:

1. **A rules file plus a roadmap in the repo.** Claude Code reads a [CLAUDE.md](http://CLAUDE.md) at the start of every session, so conventions (units, naming, what lives where, what it must never do) go there instead of being re-explained in chat. Next to it, a roadmap with a "where we are now" line and an idea parking lot: new ideas get written down, not built on the spot. That alone killed most of my drift.
2. **Acceptance checks it can't talk its way past.** Unit tests on numbers rather than screenshots: e.g. I hash each building's parts and assert that a shell hit changes only the buildings near it. And when you do judge visuals, look from more than one angle. If you only ever approve one fixed shot, you'll get things built for that one camera  (I've had walls that were only a front face). Note: It was not always Claude's fault: another model did this to me.
3. **Write decisions down the same day.** Chat context doesn't survive sessions, and stale constants do: I once had quays standing 34 cm proud because an old tile's height was still in the code after the design had moved on. On heavy design days, roughly a third of my commits are just docs.

What you're already doing (talk it through, then implement script by script) is the right core; these just keep it consistent over weeks instead of days.
